study.title: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study of GLV-12 5 mg and 10 mg once daily for 26 weeks in adults with type 2 diabetes

documents.title: Study GLV-12-301 synopsis
documents.content:
2 Synopsis
GLV-12-301 was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study of GLV-12 5 mg and 10 mg once daily, added to metformin, in adults with type 2 diabetes. Of 90 participants screened, 81 were randomised: 27 to placebo, 27 to GLV-12 5 mg and 27 to GLV-12 10 mg [T14.1.1]. In total, 73 (90.1%) participants completed the study [T14.1.1].
Efficacy: the differences from placebo in the change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 26 were -0.60 (95% CI -0.72 to -0.47) for 5 mg and -0.70 (95% CI -0.83 to -0.58) for 10 mg, both p<0.001 [T14.2.1]. The sensitivity and supplementary analyses gave similar estimates.
Safety: treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 61 participants (76.3%) [T14.3.1]. Seven participants had serious adverse events (Listing 16.2.7); one, a heart muscle infarction in the GLV-12 10 mg group, was fatal and was assessed as not related to study treatment. Light-headedness was more frequent with GLV-12 than with placebo.
Conclusion: GLV-12 5 mg and 10 mg lowered HbA1c more than placebo over 26 weeks. The main risk seen was light-headedness; the study was too small to describe uncommon risks.

documents.title: Study GLV-12-301 report body
documents.content:
1 Title page
A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group phase 3 study of the efficacy and safety of Glyvantra (GLV-12) 5 mg and 10 mg once daily in adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (GLYDE-3).
Investigational product: Glyvantra (GLV-12) film-coated tablets. Indication: type 2 diabetes mellitus inadequately controlled on metformin.
Design: randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group; 26 weeks of treatment with 4 weeks of follow-up.
Sponsor: Glyvant Pharmaceuticals (fictional), Boston, United States. Protocol GLV-12-301, version 2.0 (amendment 1). Phase 3. NCT99912301 (fictional).
First participant enrolled: 2026-01-14. Last participant completed: 2026-12-22.
Coordinating investigator: Dr Helena Vos, site 103 (fictional). Sponsor’s responsible medical officer: medical monitor, Glyvant Pharmaceuticals (fictional).
The study was conducted in accordance with ICH Good Clinical Practice, including the archiving of essential documents.
3 Table of contents
4 List of abbreviations and definitions of terms
ALT: alanine aminotransferase
ANCOVA: analysis of covariance
AST: aspartate aminotransferase
CI: confidence interval
CYP3A4: cytochrome P450 3A4
eGFR: estimated glomerular filtration rate
EST1: the primary estimand
GLYDE-3: the trial acronym of GLV-12-301
HbA1c: glycated haemoglobin
ICH: International Council for Harmonisation
LS: least squares
MMRM: mixed model for repeated measures
NCT: the ClinicalTrials.gov identifier
SAE: serious adverse event
SAP: statistical analysis plan
SD: standard deviation
SE: standard error
TEAE: treatment-emergent adverse event
ULN: upper limit of normal
5 Ethics
5.1 Independent ethics committee or institutional review board
The protocol, amendment 1, the participant information and the consent form were reviewed and approved by the independent ethics committee or institutional review board of each site before the site enrolled participants. The committees are listed in appendix 16.1.3.
5.2 Ethical conduct of the study
The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, ICH E6 Good Clinical Practice and the applicable regulatory requirements of each country.
5.3 Patient information and consent
Each participant gave written informed consent at the screening visit, before any study procedure. Participants enrolled before amendment 1 were not asked to consent again, because the amendment did not change what they were asked to do. The participant information and consent form is in appendix 16.1.3.
6 Investigators and study administrative structure
The study was run by Glyvant Pharmaceuticals (fictional) at five sites in the United States, Japan, Germany, India and Brazil. Dr Helena Vos (site 103) was the coordinating investigator. An independent data monitoring committee reviewed unblinded safety data. A central laboratory performed all laboratory tests, and an interactive response technology vendor managed randomisation and drug supply. The investigators and their affiliations are listed in appendix 16.1.4.
7 Introduction
Glyvantra (GLV-12) was an once-daily oral glucose transport modulator (a fictional class). This trial asks whether Glyvantra (GLV-12) was more effective than placebo in type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin, and how safe it was, over 26 weeks.
Identified and potential risks come from the nonclinical studies and earlier clinical trials summarised in the investigator's brochure. Each was mitigated by the eligibility criteria (section 5), the safety assessments in the schedule of activities (section 8.4) and the discontinuation rules (section 7.1).
8 Study objectives
Primary objective: to show that GLV-12 lowers HbA1c more than placebo after 26 weeks in adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin.
Secondary objective: to assess the safety and tolerability of GLV-12 5 mg and 10 mg over 26 weeks.
Primary endpoint: change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 26.
Secondary endpoint: treatment-emergent adverse events; change in ALT, AST, creatinine and fasting glucose; vital signs.
Estimand EST1: in adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (HbA1c 7.0% to 10.5%), the difference in means between GLV-12 5 mg or 10 mg once daily vs placebo for 26 weeks, added on to metformin; intercurrent events: permanent discontinuation of trial intervention (hypothetical strategy); start of rescue therapy (hypothetical strategy).
9 Investigational plan
9.1 Overall study design and plan: description
Glyvantra (GLV-12) in type 2 diabetes (GLV-12-301) was a phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group study in type 2 diabetes mellitus inadequately controlled on metformin. Participants were randomised: block randomisation 1:1:1 through an interactive response technology system. The groups were GLV-12 5 mg (GLV-12 5 mg orally once daily for 26 weeks, with metformin), GLV-12 10 mg (GLV-12 10 mg orally once daily for 26 weeks, with metformin) and Placebo (matching placebo orally once daily for 26 weeks, with metformin). Treatment lasted 26 weeks, with follow-up 4 weeks later. The study ran at 5 sites in the United States, Japan, Germany, India and Brazil, overseen by an independent data monitoring committee. The plan was to randomise 90 participants.
9.2 Discussion of study design, including the choice of control groups
A parallel group design was used because the condition could change over the treatment period and the effect was not expected to wash out quickly, so a cross-over design would not be reliable.
Placebo control was needed to distinguish the effect of the intervention from the natural course of the condition and from expectation. Participants could use rescue therapy, so no one was left without treatment.
26 weeks of treatment was the duration regulators expect for the HbA1c endpoint, as HbA1c reflects about three months of glycaemia; 4 weeks of follow-up covered the 30-day window for treatment-emergent adverse events.
9.3 Selection of study population
Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus inadequately controlled on metformin, aged 18 to 75 years, were enrolled.
9.3.1 Inclusion criteria
IN01: Adults aged 18 to 75 years with type 2 diabetes for at least 6 months
IN02: HbA1c 7.0% to 10.5% at screening
IN03: Stable metformin of at least 1500 mg a day for 12 weeks
9.3.2 Exclusion criteria
EX01: eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2
EX02: Any other glucose-lowering drug in the last 12 weeks
EX03: History of diabetic ketoacidosis
9.3.3 Removal of patients from therapy or assessment
The trial intervention was stopped permanently for a confirmed fasting glucose above 15 mmol/L, an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, ALT above 3 × ULN with total bilirubin above 2 × ULN, pregnancy, or if the investigator judges it in the participant’s interest. Participants who stopped stay in the trial and attended every visit.
A participant could withdraw at any time. Data collected until withdrawal were kept. The site asks, but cannot require, a final safety visit.
9.4 Treatments
9.4.1 Treatments administered
GLV-12 5 mg: 5 mg film-coated tablet, oral, once daily for 26 weeks (investigational).
GLV-12 10 mg: 10 mg film-coated tablet, oral, once daily for 26 weeks (investigational).
Placebo: matching placebo tablet, oral, once daily for 26 weeks (placebo).
Metformin (background): at least 1500 mg a day, the participant’s own stable dose, oral, daily (auxiliary).
9.4.2 Identity of investigational products
GLV-12 5 mg and 10 mg film-coated tablets and matching placebo tablets, made by Glyvant Pharmaceuticals (fictional). Batches: GLV-12 5 mg G5-2601, GLV-12 10 mg G10-2601 and placebo P-2601 (fictional); the batch each participant received is in appendix 16.1.6.
9.4.3 Method of assigning patients to treatment groups
Participants were randomised through the interactive response technology system on Day 1. Block randomisation 1:1:1 through an interactive response technology system. The participant, investigator, assessors and sponsor study team were blinded. The investigator could unblind a participant through the system in an emergency.
9.4.4 Selection of doses in the study
The doses were chosen from the exposure-response analysis of the earlier trial, which showed a plateau of effect at the higher dose and acceptable safety at both.
9.4.5 Selection and timing of dose for each patient
One tablet was taken by mouth each morning with water, with or without food. A missed dose was skipped if more than 12 hours late.
9.4.6 Blinding
The study was double-blind: the participants, investigators, outcomes assessors and sponsor study team did not know the assigned treatment.
9.4.7 Prior and concomitant therapy
Background therapy: metformin at the participant’s stable dose of at least 1500 mg a day, unchanged during the trial. Rescue therapy: Rescue therapy (a sulfonylurea or basal insulin, by local practice) was started for fasting glucose above 13.3 mmol/L (240 mg/dL) after Week 4 or above 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) after Week 12, confirmed on a second sample.
Prohibited: any glucose-lowering medicine other than metformin and rescue therapy, and systemic corticosteroids for more than 7 days. Strong inhibitors of CYP3A4 were prohibited because they raise GLV-12 exposure (a possible interaction). All concomitant therapy was recorded.
9.4.8 Treatment compliance
Adherence was checked by counting tablets returned at each visit; less than 80% or more than 120% of expected tablets was a deviation.
9.5 Efficacy and safety variables
9.5.1 Efficacy and safety measurements assessed and flow chart
Informed consent: Screening.
Demographics: Screening.
Eligibility criteria: Screening, Day 1.
Medical history, including diabetes history: Screening.
Vital signs (sitting blood pressure, pulse) and weight: Screening, Day 1, Week 2, Week 4, Week 8, Week 12, Week 16, Week 20, Week 26, Follow-up.
Height and oral temperature: Screening.
HbA1c (central laboratory): Screening, Week 4, Week 12, Week 26.
Central safety chemistry and fasting glucose (ALT, AST, creatinine, total cholesterol, glucose): Screening, Week 4, Week 12, Week 26.
Diabetes education session: Day 1, Week 4.
Dispense trial intervention; tablet count and adherence: Day 1, Week 4, Week 12, Week 20, Week 26.
Adverse events: throughout.
Concomitant therapy, including metformin and rescue: throughout.
End of trial status: Follow-up.
9.5.2 Appropriateness of measurements
Not applicable. The measurements are standard and validated for trials in type 2 diabetes.
9.5.3 Primary efficacy variables
The primary variable was change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 26. The primary estimand: population, adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (HbA1c 7.0% to 10.5%); treatment, GLV-12 5 mg or 10 mg once daily vs placebo for 26 weeks, added on to metformin; intercurrent events, permanent discontinuation of trial intervention handled with a hypothetical strategy (the HbA1c the participant would have had at Week 26 had they continued treatment); start of rescue therapy handled with a hypothetical strategy (the HbA1c the participant would have had without rescue; values after rescue are not used); population-level summary, difference in means.
9.5.4 Drug concentration measurements
Not applicable. Drug concentrations were not measured in this study.
9.6 Data quality assurance
Critical-to-quality factors were the primary endpoint assessment, eligibility and safety reporting. Centralised monitoring of key risk indicators and targeted on-site review focus on them.
Data were entered in a validated electronic data capture system with an audit trail; laboratory and randomisation data were transferred electronically and reconciled.
Source recorded were the medical recorded and the worksheets defined in the monitoring plan; data entered directly in the eCRF were identified in advance.
9.7 Statistical methods planned in the protocol and determination of sample size
9.7.1 Statistical and analytical plans
Analysis sets: Intent-to-treat population (all randomised participants, analysed as randomised); Safety population (all randomised participants who took at least one dose, analysed as treated).
Estimand EST1: ANCOVA of the change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 26 with treatment as a factor and baseline HbA1c as a covariate; least-squares mean differences from placebo with 95% confidence intervals. A mixed model for repeated measures (treatment, visit, treatment by visit, baseline and baseline by visit; unstructured covariance) was the supplementary analysis. Missing data: values missing after discontinuation or rescue were assumed missing at random, consistent with the hypothetical strategy. Sensitivity: placebo-based (reference-based) multiple imputation of missing Week 26 values, then ANCOVA, combined with Rubin’s rules.
Multiplicity: the two doses were tested in a fixed sequence: GLV-12 10 mg against placebo first, at two-sided 0.05; GLV-12 5 mg only if the 10 mg test was significant. This kept the familywise type I error rate at 0.05.
Adverse events were coded with MedDRA. Treatment-emergent adverse events were those starting on or after the first dose and no later than 30 days after the last dose; they were summarised by arm in the safety population, with time to the first treatment-emergent adverse event by Kaplan-Meier. Laboratory values were shown as shift tables and vital signs by analysis window.
9.7.2 Determination of sample size
A sample size of 90 randomised participants (30 per arm) gave 80% power to detect a difference of 0.8% in the change from baseline in HbA1c between a dose of GLV-12 and placebo (standard deviation 1.0%, two-sided alpha 0.05), allowing for 15% of participants without a Week 26 value.
9.8 Changes in the conduct of the study or planned analyses
Amendment 1 (protocol version 2.0, approved 2026-03-02; primary reason: change in standard of care): exclusion criterion EX01 was lowered from an eGFR below 45 to below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, because current metformin prescribing information allows metformin down to an eGFR of 30 and sites reported screening failures of otherwise eligible participants. About 40% of participants had been enrolled when it was approved.
The protocol planned to code adverse events with MedDRA; they were coded with the Study Medical Dictionary (fictional) because this training study uses it in place of the licensed dictionary.
The output of the supplementary MMRM (Table 14.2.2) is titled “primary estimand”, and the title will be corrected because the SAP names the ANCOVA as the primary analysis and the MMRM as supplementary.
10 Study patients
10.1 Disposition of patients
Of 90 participants screened, 9 were screen failures and 81 were randomised: 27 to placebo, 27 to GLV-12 5 mg and 27 to GLV-12 10 mg [T14.1.1]. Of these, 80 (98.8%) took at least one dose of study treatment. In total, 73 (90.1%) participants completed the study: 25 (92.6%) in the placebo group, 24 (88.9%) in the GLV-12 5 mg group and 24 (88.9%) in the GLV-12 10 mg group [T14.1.1]. The most common primary reasons for discontinuation were an adverse event (3 participants, 3.7%) and withdrawal by the participant (3 participants, 3.7%); 1 participant in the GLV-12 10 mg group died [T14.1.1].
10.2 Protocol deviations
No output of protocol deviations was available for this analysis; the deviations listing (16.2.2) has been requested from data management. The per-protocol set was not used for any analysis.
11 Efficacy evaluation
11.1 Data sets analysed
All randomised participants were in the intent-to-treat population, and all who took at least one dose of study treatment were in the safety population [T14.1.1]. One participant randomised to GLV-12 5 mg did not take study treatment and was excluded from the safety population [T14.1.1].
11.2 Demographic and other baseline characteristics
Of the 80 participants in the safety population, 36 (45.0%) were female and 44 (55.0%) were male [T14.1.2]. The mean (SD) age was 54.2 (12.15) years overall, and 20 participants (25.0%) were aged 65 or over [T14.1.2]. Half of the participants were Asian (40, 50.0%), and 30 (37.5%) were White [T14.1.2]. The groups were similar in age, although the GLV-12 10 mg group had more men (17, 65.4%) than the placebo group (11, 40.7%) [T14.1.2].
11.3 Measurements of treatment compliance
Not applicable. Not applicable to the training data: no drug accountability data were collected in this cut.
11.4 Efficacy results and tabulations of individual patient data
11.4.1 Analysis of efficacy
At Week 26, the LS mean change from baseline in HbA1c was -0.72% with GLV-12 5 mg and -0.83% with GLV-12 10 mg, against -0.13% with placebo [T14.2.1]. The differences from placebo were -0.60 (95% CI -0.72 to -0.47) for 5 mg and -0.70 (95% CI -0.83 to -0.58) for 10 mg, both p<0.001 [T14.2.1]. Following the fixed testing sequence, 10 mg was tested first and 5 mg second; both comparisons were significant. The placebo-based multiple imputation gave similar results: -0.56 (95% CI -0.71 to -0.40) for 5 mg and -0.62 (95% CI -0.77 to -0.47) for 10 mg [T14.2.3]. The supplementary MMRM analysis gave LS mean differences at Week 26 of -0.59 (5 mg) and -0.69 (10 mg) [T14.2.2].
11.4.2 Statistical and analytical issues
The primary analysis adjusted for baseline HbA1c, as planned [T14.2.1]. Missing Week 26 values were handled in the sensitivity analysis by placebo-based multiple imputation, which gave similar estimates [T14.2.3]. The two doses were tested in the planned fixed sequence, so no further adjustment for multiplicity was needed. The output of the supplementary MMRM is titled “primary estimand”; the SAP made it supplementary, and the title will be corrected [T14.2.2].
11.4.3 Tabulation of individual response data
Not applicable. By-patient efficacy data are in listing 16.2.6.
11.4.4 Drug dose, drug concentration and relationships to response
Not applicable. Not applicable: no dose-response, interaction or by-patient analyses were planned in the SAP.
11.4.5 Drug-drug and drug-disease interactions
Not applicable. Not applicable: no dose-response, interaction or by-patient analyses were planned in the SAP.
11.4.6 By-patient displays
Not applicable. Not applicable: no dose-response, interaction or by-patient analyses were planned in the SAP.
11.4.7 Efficacy conclusions
GLV-12 5 mg and 10 mg once daily lowered HbA1c more than placebo over 26 weeks. In the primary analysis the differences from placebo were -0.60% for 5 mg and -0.70% for 10 mg, and both comparisons were significant in the fixed testing sequence [T14.2.1]. The sensitivity analysis and the supplementary MMRM gave similar estimates, so the result does not depend on how missing data were handled.
12 Safety evaluation
12.1 Extent of exposure
The mean (SD) duration of treatment was 176.7 (22.86) days with placebo, 173.0 (36.91) days with GLV-12 5 mg and 172.5 (28.82) days with GLV-12 10 mg [T14.3.5]. In total, 47 participants (58.8%) were treated for more than 182 days, and total exposure was 38.1 participant-years [T14.3.5].
12.2 Adverse events
12.2.1 Brief summary of adverse events
Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 61 participants (76.3%): 23 (85.2%) in the placebo group, 17 (63.0%) in the GLV-12 5 mg group and 21 (80.8%) in the GLV-12 10 mg group [T14.3.1]. Adverse events led 3 participants (3.7%) to stop the study, and 1 participant in the GLV-12 10 mg group died [T14.1.1].
12.2.2 Display of adverse events
The most common events were light-headedness (16 participants, 20.0%), back pain (15, 18.8%) and fatigue (14, 17.5%) [T14.3.1]. Light-headedness was more frequent with GLV-12 10 mg (7, 26.9%) and GLV-12 5 mg (6, 22.2%) than with placebo (3, 11.1%) [T14.3.1]. Diarrhoea was reported by 6 participants (22.2%) in the placebo group, 4 (14.8%) in the GLV-12 5 mg group and 2 (7.7%) in the GLV-12 10 mg group [T14.3.1].
12.2.3 Analysis of adverse events
The median time to the first treatment-emergent adverse event was 40 days with placebo, 72 days with GLV-12 5 mg and 55 days with GLV-12 10 mg [T14.3.8]. The hazard ratios against placebo were 0.61 (95% CI 0.32 to 1.14) for 5 mg and 0.86 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.56) for 10 mg [T14.3.8]. The log-rank test across the three arms gave p=0.281 [T14.3.8].
12.2.4 Listing of adverse events by patient
12.3 Deaths, other serious adverse events and other significant adverse events
12.3.1 Listing of deaths, other serious adverse events and other significant adverse events
Seven participants had serious adverse events (Listing 16.2.7): three in the GLV-12 10 mg group (fainting, transient brain ischaemia and heart muscle infarction), two in the GLV-12 5 mg group (kidney stone and cellulitis) and two in the placebo group (pneumonia and wrist fracture). One was fatal: heart muscle infarction in a participant in the GLV-12 10 mg group (GLV-12-301-105-006), starting on Day 97; it was severe, and the investigator assessed it as not related to study treatment. The investigator assessed one serious event, fainting in the GLV-12 10 mg group on Day 102, as related to study treatment. All other serious events resolved. Their narratives are in section 12.3.2.
12.3.2 Narratives of deaths, other serious adverse events and certain other significant adverse events
Narratives follow for each participant who died, had a serious adverse event or stopped study treatment because of an adverse event, in order of participant number.
12.3.3 Analysis and discussion of deaths, other serious adverse events and other significant adverse events
Serious adverse events were reported in all three groups (Listing 16.2.7). Two serious events in the GLV-12 10 mg group affected the brain and nerves (fainting and transient brain ischaemia), and the investigator assessed the fainting as related to study treatment. Together with the more frequent light-headedness on GLV-12 [T14.3.1], this suggests that low blood pressure or low glucose on GLV-12 needs further study. The fatal heart muscle infarction was assessed as not related to study treatment.
12.4 Clinical laboratory evaluation
Most participants had normal liver tests at baseline and at Week 26 in every group [T14.3.4]. No pattern of liver test rises was seen with GLV-12. Most participants had high fasting glucose at baseline, as expected in type 2 diabetes.
12.5 Vital signs, physical findings and other observations related to safety
Systolic blood pressure fell from baseline to Week 26 in every group, with mean changes (mmHg) of -2.4 in the placebo group, -4.8 in the GLV-12 5 mg group and -9.6 in the GLV-12 10 mg group [T14.3.6]. Mean body weight fell by -0.8 kg with placebo, -1.6 kg with GLV-12 5 mg and -2.8 kg with GLV-12 10 mg [T14.3.6].
12.6 Safety conclusions
Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by a similar proportion of participants in each group [T14.3.1]. Light-headedness was more frequent on GLV-12, and the larger fall in blood pressure on GLV-12 10 mg [T14.3.6] may explain it. Seven participants had serious adverse events; the one death was assessed as not related to study treatment. The study was too small and too short to describe uncommon or late risks.
13 Discussion and overall conclusions
GLV-12 5 mg and 10 mg once daily, added to metformin, lowered HbA1c more than placebo over 26 weeks: the differences from placebo were -0.60 (95% CI -0.72 to -0.47) for 5 mg and -0.70 (95% CI -0.83 to -0.58) for 10 mg [T14.2.1]. The sensitivity analysis gave similar results, so the benefit does not depend on how missing data were handled.
The main risk seen was light-headedness, with larger falls in blood pressure on the higher dose. Seven participants had serious adverse events, and one participant on GLV-12 10 mg died of a heart muscle infarction assessed as not related to study treatment.
The main limitations are the small number of participants and the 26-week duration: uncommon or late risks could not be described. On these data, the benefit on HbA1c outweighs the risks seen; the benefit–risk balance of the 10 mg dose, with its larger effect on blood pressure, should be confirmed in a larger and longer study.
15 Reference list
ICH E3: Structure and content of clinical study reports (1995), and its Questions and Answers (R1) (2012).
ICH E9(R1): Addendum on estimands and sensitivity analysis in clinical trials (2019).
ICH E6(R3): Good clinical practice (2025).

The protocol of GLV-12-301, as approved, with its amendments.
Amendment 1 (protocol version 2.0, approved 2026-03-02; primary reason: change in standard of care): Exclusion criterion EX01 lowered from an eGFR below 45 to below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, in line with current metformin prescribing information, which allows metformin down to an eGFR of 30; sites reported screening failures of otherwise eligible participants.
